screens.title: Observer and Command Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore two complementary behavioral patterns you will use often. First, the Observer pattern gives you a publish-subscribe mechanism so a subject can notify many observers when its state changes without knowing their concrete classes. Imagine a stock price changing and many components — charts, alerts, trading rules — reacting automatically. Second, the Command pattern treats an action as an object. That encapsulation makes it possible to queue requests, log them, and implement undo and redo. Think of a remote control button that can be reprogrammed to call a different receiver operation while the invoker remains unchanged. Across the lesson you will see concise Java examples: a stock market subject with displays using Observer, and a text editor and remote control using Command. You will also study common pitfalls: observer lifecycle management and update storms, and keeping commands thin so business logic isn't leaked into execute. By the end you'll understand the roles of subject, observer, command, receiver, invoker and how to choose the right pattern for notifications versus operation management. Ready to explore practical implementations and trade-offs?

screens.title: Observer Pattern — Publish-Subscribe Model
screens.narratorSegment: The Observer pattern creates a one-to-many dependency between a subject and its observers so that when the subject changes state, all registered observers are notified automatically. At its core this is a publish-subscribe model: the subject publishes change events and observers subscribe to receive them. This separation matters because it prevents the subject from hard-wiring behavior about its dependents. Consider a stock market object that holds a price. Without Observer, every component that needs the price must be called directly by the stock object. That tightly couples the stock to each component and makes it hard to add or remove displays. With Observer, the stock only knows it has a list of observers. When setPrice is called and a change happens, the stock iterates the list and calls an update method on each observer. Concrete observers decide how to react — a chart redraws, a trading rule recalculates, a notification service composes alerts. A common misconception is that Observer automatically orders updates or prevents cascading effects. It does not: the subject simply notifies; observers may themselves change other subjects, causing chains of updates. Practical designs mitigate this with careful ordering, batching, or change filtering. In short, Observer separates who changed from who reacts, reducing coupling and improving extensibility.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Observer is a publish-subscribe mechanism creating a one-to-many relationship so subjects notify observers of state changes without knowing their concrete types.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Observer Pattern
Definition • Publish-Subscribe
What it is

A subject maintains observers and notifies them on state changes by calling an update method. Observers register and unregister at runtime.

When to use
When many components must react to changes and you want to add or remove observers without changing the subject.
Common misconception
Observer does not manage update order or prevent cascading updates; you must design for those concerns separately.
Key takeaway
Decouples notification producers from consumers, improving extensibility but requiring lifecycle care.
Concrete example: stock price
Subject: StockMarket holds price and a list of StockObserver. When price changes it calls notifyObservers.
Observers: StockDisplay and TradingAlgo implement update and decide how to react, such as redrawing or re-evaluating rules.
Lifecycle: registerObserver adds to the list, removeObserver removes it. Failing to remove leads to memory leaks.
Key Takeaway

Observer provides a lightweight event bus per subject, but you must manage ordering, batching, and observer lifecycle to avoid unexpected behavior.

screens.title: Implementing Observer in Java
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Java example that implements the Observer pattern. The pattern has two main interfaces: a StockObserver with an update method, and a StockSubject with register, remove, and notify operations. In the concrete subject, StockMarket, maintain an internal list of observers. When setPrice is called and the price actually changes, call notifyObservers to iterate and invoke update on each observer, passing the stock symbol and new price. Observers like StockDisplay implement update and perform their own behavior, such as printing a message or refreshing a view. A practical point: always check whether the new state differs from the previous state before notifying; this prevents unnecessary update storms. Another practical detail is safe iteration: if observers might unregister themselves during notification, avoid ConcurrentModification by iterating over a shallow copy of the list or using a safe iterator. For lifecycle, ensure observers remove themselves when they are destroyed. In many Java apps, weak references or explicit unregister calls are used to prevent leaks. Run a quick demo by registering two displays, changing the price a few times, then removing one observer and changing the price again to confirm only the remaining observer receives updates. This walkthrough shows how to wire subject and observers for reliable event propagation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Java Observer Walkthrough
Live coding demo style
Key classes
  • StockObserver: update(String symbol, double price)
  • StockSubject: registerObserver, removeObserver, notifyObservers
  • StockMarket: concrete subject, keeps list and calls notify when setPrice changes
Practical tips
Only notify on actual change. Iterate over a copy of the observer list to avoid concurrent modification if observers unregister during notify.
// Observer Interface
interface StockObserver { 
  void update(String stockSymbol, double price);
}

// Subject: register/remove/notify
interface StockSubject {
  void registerObserver(StockObserver o);
  void removeObserver(StockObserver o);
  void notifyObservers();
}

// Key: notify only when price changed
class StockMarket implements StockSubject {
  private List<StockObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>();
  private double price;
  public void setPrice(double newPrice) {
    if (this.price != newPrice) {
      this.price = newPrice;
      notifyObservers();
    }
  }
  // register/remove/notify implementations omitted for brevity
}
Example run

Register two displays, setPrice twice, remove one, then setPrice again to confirm only the remaining observer reacts.

screens.title: Observer Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Using Observer brings clarity but also responsibility. One frequent pitfall is observer lifecycle mismanagement: if observers register and are not removed when they are no longer in use, the subject keeps strong references and you can get memory leaks. A best practice is to unregister observers explicitly when they are disposed, or use weak references where appropriate. Another problem is the update storm. A single subject change can cascade if observers change other subjects or trigger heavy operations. To mitigate this, filter notifications so observers receive only relevant events, or batch updates and emit a single consolidated notification. Also consider the cost of notifying many observers synchronously: if notification work is heavy, push processing to background threads or schedule work through a queue. When iterating observers, prefer iterating over a snapshot of the list to prevent concurrent modification errors when an observer unregisters itself during notification. Finally, avoid embedding complex logic in observers that is unrelated to reaction; keep observers focused on responding to state changes and delegate heavy work to other components. These practices make Observer reliable in production systems.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Observer Pitfalls
Lifecycle • Performance • Correctness
Common mistakes
  • Not unregistering observers, causing memory leaks.
  • Allowing cascading updates that lead to unexpected state changes.
  • Synchronous heavy work on notification thread, blocking important tasks.
Best practices
Unregister observers on teardown, use weak references if appropriate, snapshot lists for safe iteration, and batch or offload heavy work.
Check your understanding
  1. How would you prevent observers from causing memory leaks in a long-running app?
  2. What strategies reduce the impact of cascading updates?
  3. When is it appropriate to process notifications asynchronously?
Pro Tip

Favor clear contracts: observers should expect only well-defined event payloads so unexpected side effects are minimized.

screens.title: Command Pattern — Encapsulating Requests
screens.narratorSegment: The Command pattern encapsulates a request as an object. That single idea unlocks several capabilities: parameterizing clients with different requests; queuing, logging, or retrying commands; and implementing undo by storing prior state in the command. The pattern defines a Command interface, one or more Concrete Command classes that implement execute and often undo, a Receiver that performs the real work, an Invoker that triggers the command, and a Client that assembles the pieces. Think of a remote control: each button is an invoker slot configured with a Command object. Pressing the button runs execute on that command, and the invoker doesn't need to know what the command does. A concrete example from a text editor: the Open command saves previous content before loading new content so undo can restore the prior state. A common mistake is letting execute grow large and absorb business logic; instead commands should delegate to receivers and keep state for undo small and focused. Command is particularly useful when you need to record actions, support undo, or allow runtime configuration of operations. Command Pattern — Encapsulating Requests means command turns actions into objects so invokers can execute, queue, or undo them without knowing their implementation.. In practical terms, treat actions as objects for flexible invocation and undo. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Command Pattern
Encapsulate • Queue • Undo
Pattern roles
  • Command interface: execute() and optional undo()
  • Concrete Command: binds receiver and operation
  • Receiver: performs actual work
  • Invoker: triggers command without knowing details
Analogy
A remote control button holds a Command object; you can reassign a button without changing the remote code.
Concrete example: text editor
Open, Save, Copy, and Paste can be commands. An Open command can store previous content for undo; a Save command may refuse to implement undo in a simple form. Keep undo responsibilities explicit and minimal.
Key takeaway

Commands standardize invocation and enable undo and scheduling, but they must delegate work to receivers and keep execute minimal.

screens.title: Command Roles: Client, Invoker, Receiver
screens.narratorSegment: Successful Command pattern use depends on clear responsibilities. The Client assembles concrete command objects and binds them to receivers; it configures the invoker with those commands. The Invoker is typically part of the UI or a scheduler: it stores command references in slots and triggers execute when a user presses a button or when a scheduler runs. The Concrete Command contains references to the receiver and any state required to execute or undo. It delegates the actual work to the receiver, preserving the single-responsibility principle. The Receiver contains domain logic — for example, a TextEditorReceiver knows how to open, save, copy, and paste content. Keeping business logic in the receiver prevents commands from becoming monolithic. For undo, a command must capture the minimal prior state needed to revert its changes. For example, an Open command may save the previous document content before loading a new one; calling undo restores that content. For queuing or logging, invokers can store command objects and replay them later or persist them. Recognize the trade-off: the more state a command stores for undo, the heavier it becomes. Design commands to be as lightweight as possible while still enabling correct undo behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Command Roles
Client • Invoker • Command • Receiver
Client

Constructs concrete commands and binds them to receivers. It configures invokers, deciding what command goes in which slot.

Invoker
Holds references to commands and triggers their execute method. Examples: a menu, a button, a scheduler.
Concrete Command & Receiver

Concrete commands store any state needed for execution and undo, then call the appropriate receiver methods to do the work. The receiver encapsulates domain behavior.

Design note

Keep commands thin: complex business rules belong in receivers. Only keep undo state that is strictly necessary.

screens.title: Command Pattern in Java — TextEditor Example
screens.narratorSegment: We'll step through the text editor example to see Command in practice. The Receiver class, TextEditorReceiver, holds the document content and methods like open, save, copy, and paste. The EditorCommand interface defines execute and undo. The OpenCommand stores the editor reference and the previous content. On execute it saves previousContent then calls receiver. open, and on undo it restores the saved previousContent. The SaveCommand may implement execute to call receiver. save and provide a no-op or informative undo because saving may be irreversible in a simple model. When you wire the invoker, such as a Menu class, setCommand installs a command in a slot; pressing the slot calls execute and pushes the command onto an undo stack if undo is supported. Implementing undo requires you to decide how much prior state to capture: for text content it may be simple, but for operations that change external systems you must design compensating actions carefully. A common mistake is putting domain logic in execute; instead delegate to receiver methods that encapsulate behavior. Running the demo: execute OpenCommand, inspect editor content, call undo on the last command, and confirm the previous content is restored. This sequence makes the benefits and limitations of command-based undo clear.

keyIdea.text: Store minimal prior state inside the command to reverse effects; keep business rules in the receiver and keep commands as coordinators.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › TextEditor Commands
Execute • Undo
Receiver: TextEditorReceiver
Holds content and implements open, save, copy, paste. Commands call these methods; the receiver keeps domain logic centralized.
Undo policy
Decide per-command how to undo. For Open, store previous content. For Save, you may log a warning if undo is not supported in the simple model.
// Command interface
interface EditorCommand { 
  void execute();
  void undo();
}

// OpenCommand saves state, executes open, and can undo
class OpenCommand implements EditorCommand {
  private TextEditorReceiver editor;
  private String previousContent;
  public OpenCommand(TextEditorReceiver editor) { this.editor = editor; }
  public void execute() {
    previousContent = editor.getContent();
    editor.open();
  }
  public void undo() {
    editor.setContent(previousContent);
  }
}
Try this

Execute OpenCommand, then call undo to see previous content restored. Consider what state must be saved for more complex operations.

screens.title: Observer vs Command — When to Choose Which
screens.narratorSegment: Observer and Command solve different problems and are chosen for different needs. Observer addresses event distribution: when you want a subject to broadcast state changes to multiple listeners, choose Observer. It excels in UI updates, event-driven systems, and decoupling producers from many consumers. Command addresses operation encapsulation: when you need to represent requests as first-class objects for queuing, logging, or undo, choose Command. Their strengths differ: Observer simplifies registration and notification, while Command centralizes operation invocation and supports undo stacks. Trade-offs exist: Observer can cause cascading updates and lifecycle management challenges; Command can bloat if execute contains complex business logic or stores too much undo state. They can also be combined: observers may enqueue commands in response to notifications, or commands may notify observers after execution. Consider performance and complexity: large observer graphs require batching and careful ordering, while command-heavy designs require careful undo strategies and possibly persistent logs. In practice, ask which aspect is primary — distribution of change or encapsulation of an action — then apply the appropriate pattern, with attention to the pitfalls we've discussed. Observer vs Command — When to Choose Which means observer for broadcasting state changes to many listeners; command for representing operations as objects to enable undo, queuing, and configurable invocation.. In practical terms, a side-by-side comparison of goals, strengths, and common trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Observer and Command solve different problems and are chosen for different needs. Observer addresses event distribution: when you want a subject to broadcast state changes to multiple listeners, choose Observer. It excels in UI updates, event-driven systems, and decoupling producers from many consumers. Command addresses operation encapsulation: when you need to represent requests as first-class objects for queuing, logging, or undo, choose Command. Their strengths differ: Observer simplifies registration and notification, while Command centralizes operation invocation and supports undo stacks. Trade-offs exist: Observer can cause cascading updates and lifecycle management challenges; Command can bloat if execute contains complex business logic or stores too much undo state. They can also be combined: observers may enqueue commands in response to notifications, or commands may notify observers after execution. Consider performance and complexity: large observer graphs require batching and careful ordering, while command-heavy designs require careful undo strategies and possibly persistent logs. In practice, ask which aspect is primary — distribution of change or encapsulation of an action — then apply the appropriate pattern, with attention to the pitfalls we've discussed. Observer vs Command — When to Choose Which means observer for broadcasting state changes to many listeners; command for representing operations as objects to enable undo, queuing, and configurable invocation.. In practical terms, a side-by-side comparison of goals, strengths, and common trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Observer vs Command
Goals • Strengths • Trade-offs
Observer — broadcast
  • Goal: notify many listeners on state changes
  • Strength: low coupling between subject and observers
  • Trade-offs: lifecycle, update storms, ordering
Example
StockMarket notifies displays, trading algorithms, and notification services.
Command — encapsulate
  • Goal: represent actions as objects for undo, queues, and reconfiguration
  • Strength: consistent invocation, undo stacks, and logging
  • Trade-offs: potential bloat from storing undo state or embedding business logic
Example
RemoteControl triggers LightOnCommand or StereoOnCommand without knowing receiver details.
Combined use

You can combine patterns: an observer reacting to an event may enqueue commands for later execution, or a command may notify observers after changing application state.

screens.title: Hands-on: Home Automation with Command
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on scenario asks you to implement the Command pattern in a home automation context. Your RemoteControl is the invoker with multiple slots. Receivers are devices like Light and Stereo with methods on and off. Create a Command interface with execute, then implement LightOnCommand, LightOffCommand, StereoOnCommand, and StereoOffCommand; each concrete command receives a device instance in its constructor and delegates to its corresponding receiver methods. Configure the remote by assigning on and off commands to slots. When testing, press the on button to call execute and observe the device method output. Extend the exercise by implementing a simple undo: store the last executed command in the remote and add an undo method that calls undo on that command. For volume control, implement a StereoVolumeUpCommand that captures an increment and delegates to setVolume on the receiver; be mindful that setVolume may need access to current volume. A common pitfall is assuming undo is automatic; you must design each command to save sufficient state to restore the previous condition. This activity helps cement how invoker, command, and receiver collaborate and shows how commands make the invoker flexible and extensible.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore two complementary behavioral patterns you will use often. First, the Observer pattern gives you a publish-subscribe mechanism so a subject can notify many observers when its state changes without knowing their concrete classes. Imagine a stock price changing and many components — charts, alerts, trading rules — reacting automatically. Second, the Command pattern treats an action as an object. That encapsulation makes it possible to queue requests, log them, and implement undo and redo. Think of a remote control button that can be reprogrammed to call a different receiver operation while the invoker remains unchanged. Across the lesson you will see concise Java examples: a stock market subject with displays using Observer, and a text editor and remote control using Command. You will also study common pitfalls: observer lifecycle management and update storms, and keeping commands thin so business logic isn't leaked into execute. By the end you'll understand the roles of subject, observer, command, receiver, invoker and how to choose the right pattern for notifications versus operation management. Ready to explore practical implementations and trade-offs?

This chapter has clear, practical goals. First, you will be able to explain the publish-subscribe mechanism of the Observer pattern and why it matters for event handling. That means describing how a subject maintains a list of observers and delivers notifications without depending on concrete observer classes. Second, you'll implement Observer in Java: register and remove observers, trigger notify calls, and reason about lifecycle to avoid leaks. Third, you'll understand how the Command pattern encapsulates a request as an object. This gives you a structured way to queue requests, log actions, and implement undo or redo. Fourth, you will apply Command to design flexible systems by separating invoker and receiver responsibilities so that the same invoker can execute different actions without change. Each objective is tied to a practical example: a stock market notifying displays and a remote control commanding devices. Keep an eye out for trade-offs: observers simplify notification but can cascade updates; commands simplify action management but can hide complex state if execute becomes heavy. These skills will let you design components that are easy to extend and test. Which objective feels the most urgent for your next project?

On this second objectives slide we focus on hands-on outcomes. You will implement and test the Observer example in Java, creating a StockMarket subject and multiple StockDisplay observers, then run the sequence to see notifications trigger. You will also implement Command for a small home automation remote control: define Command interfaces, create concrete on and off commands for Light and Stereo receivers, configure the remote, and verify invocation. We'll practice a simple undo flow for the Open command in the editor example to show how a command can save prior state and restore it on undo. Finally, you will learn to evaluate trade-offs: how observer registries can create memory leaks when observers are not removed, and how command execute methods can become containers for business logic if not designed thinly. Each objective includes a micro-check: run the demo, trigger a state change, and observe which objects react, then swap a command at a remote slot and confirm the invoker still works. These are the practical outcomes you will be assessed on.

The Observer pattern creates a one-to-many dependency between a subject and its observers so that when the subject changes state, all registered observers are notified automatically. At its core this is a publish-subscribe model: the subject publishes change events and observers subscribe to receive them. This separation matters because it prevents the subject from hard-wiring behavior about its dependents. Consider a stock market object that holds a price. Without Observer, every component that needs the price must be called directly by the stock object. That tightly couples the stock to each component and makes it hard to add or remove displays. With Observer, the stock only knows it has a list of observers. When setPrice is called and a change happens, the stock iterates the list and calls an update method on each observer. Concrete observers decide how to react — a chart redraws, a trading rule recalculates, a notification service composes alerts. A common misconception is that Observer automatically orders updates or prevents cascading effects. It does not: the subject simply notifies; observers may themselves change other subjects, causing chains of updates. Practical designs mitigate this with careful ordering, batching, or change filtering. In short, Observer separates who changed from who reacts, reducing coupling and improving extensibility.

Let's walk through the Java example that implements the Observer pattern. The pattern has two main interfaces: a StockObserver with an update method, and a StockSubject with register, remove, and notify operations. In the concrete subject, StockMarket, maintain an internal list of observers. When setPrice is called and the price actually changes, call notifyObservers to iterate and invoke update on each observer, passing the stock symbol and new price. Observers like StockDisplay implement update and perform their own behavior, such as printing a message or refreshing a view. A practical point: always check whether the new state differs from the previous state before notifying; this prevents unnecessary update storms. Another practical detail is safe iteration: if observers might unregister themselves during notification, avoid ConcurrentModification by iterating over a shallow copy of the list or using a safe iterator. For lifecycle, ensure observers remove themselves when they are destroyed. In many Java apps, weak references or explicit unregister calls are used to prevent leaks. Run a quick demo by registering two displays, changing the price a few times, then removing one observer and changing the price again to confirm only the remaining observer receives updates. This walkthrough shows how to wire subject and observers for reliable event propagation.

Using Observer brings clarity but also responsibility. One frequent pitfall is observer lifecycle mismanagement: if observers register and are not removed when they are no longer in use, the subject keeps strong references and you can get memory leaks. A best practice is to unregister observers explicitly when they are disposed, or use weak references where appropriate. Another problem is the update storm. A single subject change can cascade if observers change other subjects or trigger heavy operations. To mitigate this, filter notifications so observers receive only relevant events, or batch updates and emit a single consolidated notification. Also consider the cost of notifying many observers synchronously: if notification work is heavy, push processing to background threads or schedule work through a queue. When iterating observers, prefer iterating over a snapshot of the list to prevent concurrent modification errors when an observer unregisters itself during notification. Finally, avoid embedding complex logic in observers that is unrelated to reaction; keep observers focused on responding to state changes and delegate heavy work to other components. These practices make Observer reliable in production systems.

The Command pattern encapsulates a request as an object. That single idea unlocks several capabilities: parameterizing clients with different requests; queuing, logging, or retrying commands; and implementing undo by storing prior state in the command. The pattern defines a Command interface, one or more Concrete Command classes that implement execute and often undo, a Receiver that performs the real work, an Invoker that triggers the command, and a Client that assembles the pieces. Think of a remote control: each button is an invoker slot configured with a Command object. Pressing the button runs execute on that command, and the invoker doesn't need to know what the command does. A concrete example from a text editor: the Open command saves previous content before loading new content so undo can restore the prior state. A common mistake is letting execute grow large and absorb business logic; instead commands should delegate to receivers and keep state for undo small and focused. Command is particularly useful when you need to record actions, support undo, or allow runtime configuration of operations. Command Pattern — Encapsulating Requests means command turns actions into objects so invokers can execute, queue, or undo them without knowing their implementation.. In practical terms, treat actions as objects for flexible invocation and undo. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Successful Command pattern use depends on clear responsibilities. The Client assembles concrete command objects and binds them to receivers; it configures the invoker with those commands. The Invoker is typically part of the UI or a scheduler: it stores command references in slots and triggers execute when a user presses a button or when a scheduler runs. The Concrete Command contains references to the receiver and any state required to execute or undo. It delegates the actual work to the receiver, preserving the single-responsibility principle. The Receiver contains domain logic — for example, a TextEditorReceiver knows how to open, save, copy, and paste content. Keeping business logic in the receiver prevents commands from becoming monolithic. For undo, a command must capture the minimal prior state needed to revert its changes. For example, an Open command may save the previous document content before loading a new one; calling undo restores that content. For queuing or logging, invokers can store command objects and replay them later or persist them. Recognize the trade-off: the more state a command stores for undo, the heavier it becomes. Design commands to be as lightweight as possible while still enabling correct undo behavior.

We'll step through the text editor example to see Command in practice. The Receiver class, TextEditorReceiver, holds the document content and methods like open, save, copy, and paste. The EditorCommand interface defines execute and undo. The OpenCommand stores the editor reference and the previous content. On execute it saves previousContent then calls receiver. open, and on undo it restores the saved previousContent. The SaveCommand may implement execute to call receiver. save and provide a no-op or informative undo because saving may be irreversible in a simple model. When you wire the invoker, such as a Menu class, setCommand installs a command in a slot; pressing the slot calls execute and pushes the command onto an undo stack if undo is supported. Implementing undo requires you to decide how much prior state to capture: for text content it may be simple, but for operations that change external systems you must design compensating actions carefully. A common mistake is putting domain logic in execute; instead delegate to receiver methods that encapsulate behavior. Running the demo: execute OpenCommand, inspect editor content, call undo on the last command, and confirm the previous content is restored. This sequence makes the benefits and limitations of command-based undo clear.
